summary: Introductory hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, tuning generation params, and retry/backoff patterns. Customer is evaluating Redwood for a HIPAA-adjacent clinical communications product; primary concerns were latency, cost, and security (data residency/SOC2). AE + SE walked through live examples, parameter tradeoffs, and recommended default backoff strategy. Agreed next steps include benchmarks with customer prompts and follow-up scoping for a pilot.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. Today Priya and I will show a quick hosted API walk-through focused on streaming and backoff patterns.
[00:12] Maya Solis: Hi Alex, thanks. Budget and timeline are tight so we want the shortest path to a pilot. We use short chat responses, usually under 150 tokens, but occasionally have longer visit notes.
[00:25] Dan Rivera: Also high priority is response time under 300ms median for short responses, and predictable tail latency.
[00:35] Priya Rao: Great, quick note, those constraints map well to our hosted API — we can tune batching, kv cache, and use a lower-capacity variant for short responses. We'll demo streaming so you can see partial token delivery.
[00:48] Alex Chen: Alright, starting a live example — calling the chat endpoint, streaming enabled. Temperature 0.0, top_p 1.0, max_tokens 150.
[01:03] (sound of typing)
[01:10] Priya Rao: You'll see the stream chunks come in as delta tokens. Streaming reduces perceived latency because the client can render partial tokens before the final response completes.
[01:22] Maya Solis: The transcript often needs to be saved — how do you handle partial writes? Any ordering guarantees?
[01:31] Priya Rao: Order is preserved. If a connection drops we provide a final status code in the event stream; we recommend idempotency tokens on requests to resume or deduplicate.
[01:45] Dan Rivera: If a chunk is lost and connection is resumed, do we get the remainder or must we re-request?
[01:53] Priya Rao: You'd typically re-issue the request with same idempotency token. If you want exact resume you need session-level KV cache which is available on Dedicated / Private today; hosted has prefix caching to avoid re-computing full context in many cases.
[02:08] Maya Solis: Hmm ok. Security — we are HIPAA-adjacent. What about data residency and retention?
[02:16] Alex Chen: For hosted, we have region controls and configurable retention windows; we can also offer Private deployment for stricter controls. We'll share SOC 2 and encryption details after the call.
[02:28] Lena Ortiz: Please include KMS/HSM options in that doc.
[02:33] Alex Chen: Will do. Back to retries — Priya, show the backoff example?
[02:37] Priya Rao: Yes. Typical pattern: linear retries for idempotent requests, exponential backoff with jitter for streaming where you want to avoid thundering herd. Example: initial retry after 200ms, then 500ms, 1s, 2s capped at 8s. Also include a max total retry budget like 10s.
[02:56] Dan Rivera: Do you expose retry headers so we can see server-side hinted backoff or congestion signals?
[03:03] Priya Rao: We expose simple rate-limit headers and a token-cost estimate in responses. For more advanced signals we can hook into tracing and console dashboards.
[03:14] Maya Solis: About parameters — what are recommended defaults for short deterministic responses?
[03:20] Priya Rao: For deterministic: temperature 0.0, top_p 1.0, frequency_penalty low. For diversity you increase temp to 0.7. Also set max_tokens tight to avoid runaway costs, and use stop sequences for structured outputs.
[03:36] Alex Chen: We demo sending a request with temp 0.0 vs 0.8 so you can see differences.
[03:43] (demo plays, audible keyboard)
[04:05] Maya Solis: The higher temp looks more verbose and sometimes invents details — we need high precision so default 0.0 makes sense.
[04:12] Priya Rao: Also talk about beam and sampling — our API focuses on sampling controls, not beams; so you manage diversity mainly with temperature/top_p.
[04:24] Dan Rivera: On cost — if we use streaming and smaller models for short replies, what's the unit economics?
[04:31] Alex Chen: Cost roughly proportional to tokens processed; streaming doesn't add extra token cost but reduces latency. Using a smaller model for short answers reduces per-token compute cost. We can provide a sample cost model based on your prompt lengths.
[04:45] Maya Solis: Can you fall back automatically to a cheaper model when latency spikes or capacity is constrained?
[04:52] Priya Rao: Yes, smart routing policies let you set fallbacks. You can route by latency SLO or cost threshold. The runtime can automatically use a compatible quantized variant if the primary is unavailable.
[05:05] Dan Rivera: If fallback is used, how do we detect regression in response quality?
[05:11] Priya Rao: Console exposes per-model evals and quality monitoring — we can tie alerts to evaluation sets so you see when fallbacks degrade quality beyond a threshold.
[05:22] Maya Solis: Good. For retries, are there built-in client SDK helpers?
[05:27] Priya Rao: Yes, our SDK includes retry wrappers and sample code for exponential backoff and idempotency tokens, plus streaming re-connect helpers. We'll email the examples.
[05:38] Alex Chen: There's also a small demo of token-level cost in the Console; it shows how much each request consumed so you can attribute cost.
[05:46] (short pause)
[06:00] Dan Rivera: One of the edge use-cases — sometimes the model starts generating PHI-like placeholders; can you scrub predictions or redact?
[06:09] Priya Rao: We support response filters and safety hooks; you can run a post-generation classifier or rule-based scrubber. For sensitive environments we recommend on-prem or Private with additional processing steps.
[06:22] Maya Solis: For the POC, what would success criteria look like?
[06:27] Alex Chen: We suggested: median latency under 300ms for short responses, <150ms tail improvement with streaming, cost per 1k responses under an agreed threshold, and compatibility with your retention/KMS requirements.
[06:42] (customer notes)
[06:55] Lena Ortiz: We'll need legal + security sign-off — can you send an initial compliance pack?
[07:01] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll send SOC 2, encryption, network diagrams, and KMS info.
[07:07] Dan Rivera: Can we do a short benchmark — send 1000 short prompts and measure latency?
[07:13] Priya Rao: Absolutely. We'll run that with your prompts against our hosted instance and return a spreadsheet with per-request timing and errors.
[07:24] Maya Solis: Great. A technical question about streaming chunk size — is it tunable client-side or server decides?
[07:31] Priya Rao: Server decides chunk flush frequency based on buffer and tokenization boundaries, but client-side you can request smaller max_chunk_bytes in some SDKs; note too small chunks increase overhead.
[07:45] Dan Rivera: What's the typical chunk size in tokens?
[07:48] Priya Rao: Usually 4–12 tokens per chunk for English, but depends on model tokenization and response pacing.
[07:57] Alex Chen: We should pause demo and look at the retry header example in the docs. Priya, can you share your screen?
[08:04] (screen change)
[08:10] Priya Rao: Here's an example header: x-redwood-rate-limit: 1200, x-redwood-retry-after-ms: 500. Combine those with client-side backoff.
[08:20] Maya Solis: If we get 429 spikes, is circuit breaking recommended?
[08:24] Priya Rao: Yes, circuit breaking plus exponential backoff with jitter is recommended to protect both sides. We also provide per-tenant quota controls.
[08:33] Dan Rivera: Are there examples for graceful UX when stream cuts out mid-message?
[08:37] Alex Chen: UX patterns we recommend: show partial text with a spinner and, on reconnect, indicate message status (delivered/failed). Also store intermediate tokens server-side in Dedicated/Private for better resume.
[08:52] Maya Solis: On the SDKs — do you support browser-based streaming securely?
[08:57] Priya Rao: Browser streaming is supported via SSE/WebSocket patterns; recommend proxying through your backend to avoid exposing keys.
[09:07] Dan Rivera: For our mobile app we want low-power consumption — is streaming more battery-friendly than waiting?
[09:13] Priya Rao: Streaming typically allows you to render fast and then stop receiving which can save time, but it keeps the connection open; it's a tradeoff. We'll help tune keep-alive and chunk sizing.
[09:26] (brief cross talk)
[09:40] Alex Chen: Quick note on truncation — if reply hits max_tokens we return a truncation flag; we suggest checking that flag and optionally issuing a follow-up to continue generation.
[09:53] Maya Solis: Ok. Are there any rate-limit tiers we should be aware of for a POC?
[09:59] Alex Chen: For hosted POC we'll give a comfortable quota; if you need sustained QPS we'll discuss Dedicated reservation.
[10:08] Dan Rivera: Can you put in the follow-up email an example of a canary rollout? We're worried about quality regressions when we flip models.
[10:16] Priya Rao: Sure — typical canary: 5% traffic to new model for 24–48 hours, monitor evaluation metrics and user-facing KPIs, then ramp. Our console supports that rollout pattern.
[10:29] Maya Solis: I have one more question: do you provide server-side batching? We want to avoid sending 100 parallel calls if we can coalesce.
[10:36] Priya Rao: The runtime does continuous batching where possible to improve GPU utilization while preserving latency SLOs; customers can set batching configuration in Console for Dedicated. Hosted runtime batches opportunistically.
[10:49] Dan Rivera: Anything else on observability?
[10:52] Alex Chen: Per-route token cost, traces, and model-level eval dashboards. We'll hand over a sample dashboard link.
[11:02] (longer demo and Q&A segment continues, omitted for brevity)
[38:12] Priya Rao: Wrapping up notes — agreed actions: we'll run the latency benchmark and share docs.
[38:20] Maya Solis: Thanks, that was very helpful. We'll compile prompts and send them.
[38:26] Dan Rivera: Thanks Alex, Priya.
[38:30] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and schedule.
[38:35] (meeting ends)
additional_notes: Transcript has occasional misheard words (typical automated transcription), some technical terms simplified. Customer is HIPAA-adjacent and emphasized SOC 2 + KMS. Redwood AE/SE pair present. Agreed pilot to measure latency/cost with sample prompts.
